newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil pays price for mining sale delay, official says.
newsitem.headline: Brazil pays price for mining sale delay, official says.

text.p: Brazil will start losing money this week because of the delay in the sale of the state-owned mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD), the head of the National Development Bank (BNDES) was quoted as saying Sunday.
Latin America's largest privatisation so far had originally been set for April 29 but has been rescheduled several times because of a flood of court injunctions.

Had the sale been allowed to go ahead as originally planned, the government would have received at least $2.8 billion on Monday, BNDES president Luiz Carlos Mendonca de Barros told the Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper.
"From Monday, the Treasury starts to suffer a real loss because the auction has not taken place," Mendonca de Barros said.

"If the sale had taken place on April 29...the Treasury would have had at least three billion reais ($2.8 billion) in its coffers and these funds would have been used to reduce debts," he told the newspaper.
The BNDES is examining whether there is a case to lodge its own lawsuit because of losses suffered by the delay, he added.
The bank has said it was ready to hold the sale on May 5 but a high court judge who is considering a government appeal against the lawsuits has said his decision may come on May 6, at the earliest.

In the Folha interview, Mendonca de Barros said the sale could take place this week as long as the legal problems were resolved but he did not want to say exactly which day he thought it was likely to happen.
Seen as the key test to President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's commitment to state reform, the sale of CVRD has raised considerable opposition from nationalists and leftists.
Opponents have accused the government of selling for a pittance the country's mineral wealth such as the Carajas iron ore mine which contains the biggest iron ore deposit in the world.

Two groups have registered to bid for a 45 percent voting stake in CVRD, one led by local steel firm CSN and another headed by Brazil's largest private industrial conglomerate Grupo Votorantim and South Africa's Anglo-American Corp.
While the Votorantim and Anglo-American group is well-defined, the CSN-led group is continuing to negotiate with a number of companies.
Local Jornal do Brasil newspaper said Sunday that Citibank was the latest new member after deciding to contribute to offshore investment fund Opportunity Asset Management.
CSN officials could not immediately be reached to confirm the report.

In addition to Opportunity, the CSN-led consortium contains four local pension funds and NationsBank Corp. while South African mining company Gencor has signed a letter of intent to join, should the group win the auction.
